+        if len(ids) < 2:
+            return ids
+        # ranks[i] is the merge index of the pair (ids[i], ids[i+1]), or inf
+        # when it cannot be merged; only the ranks next to a merge change
+        inf = float("inf")
+        ranks = []
+        append = ranks.append
+        prev = ids[0]
+        for curr in islice(ids, 1, None):
+            nexts = merge_lookup[prev]
+            append(inf if nexts is None else nexts.get(curr, inf))
+            prev = curr
+        while ranks:
+            # find the pair with the lowest merge index (first occurrence)
+            best_idx = min(ranks)

+                break # nothing else can be merged anymore
+            i = ranks.index(best_idx)
+            best_p0 = ids[i]

+            while True:
+                ids[i:i+2] = [best_idx]

actions.reason:
I found nothing that improves encode_ir by the required 1%. All three evaluations gave identical outputs:
1. Deferring the unicodedata and Counter imports, and calling compiled_pattern.findall directly, measured 0.9980. The regex module seems to import those modules already, so deferring them saves almost nothing.
2. Rewriting RegexTokenizer._encode_chunk to keep a list of per-position merge ranks and update only the neighbours of each merge measured 1.0904, which is worse. Part of the cost was a ValueError raised on every merge pass.
3. Removing that exception path brought it to 1.0354, still worse. The chunks are short enough that bookkeeping costs more than the per-pass rescan it replaces.
Next ideas, not tried yet: a flat integer-keyed merge lookup in the scan loop, or a cheaper fast path for 2-3 byte chunks.

journal.text:
I tried to cut encode_ir in the minbpe lineage. First I deferred the unicodedata and Counter imports in minbpe/base.py and minbpe/basic.py and called compiled_pattern.findall directly in minbpe/regex.py. Then I rewrote RegexTokenizer._encode_chunk to keep a list of per-position merge ranks.

The first change measured encode_ir ratio 0.9980 against a required 0.9900, so it was rejected. The _encode_chunk rewrite measured 1.0904. A revised version of it measured 1.0354. Both were slower and both were rejected. All three runs gave identical outputs. train_ir stayed near parity, at 1.0002, 1.0011 and 1.0006.

I believe the regex module already imports unicodedata and Counter, so deferring them saves almost nothing. Keeping per-position rank bookkeeping in Python costs more than the simple pair rescan it replaces. I submitted no candidate.

Next I would profile encode before editing, to see how much time is in findall and how much is in the merge loop. Only then would I choose a target.
